stem: A model trained on emails labelled 'spam' or 'not spam' is an example of:

options.text: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Self-supervised learning

explanation_after: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples (input → target). The spam/not-spam labels provide the supervision signal.

stem: K-Means clustering is an example of which type of learning?

options.text: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning

explanation_after: K-Means groups data into clusters without any labels — it discovers structure in unlabelled data, which is the definition of unsupervised learning.

stem: In reinforcement learning, what does the agent learn from?

options.text: Labelled input-output pairs provided by humans
Reward signals received after taking actions in an environment
Unlabelled data clusters
Pre-trained model weights

explanation_after: RL agents receive rewards (positive for good actions, negative for bad) and learn to maximise cumulative reward through trial and error. No labelled training data is required.

stem: GPT's pre-training (predicting the next word in text) is an example of:

options.text: Supervised learning with human-annotated data
Self-supervised learning — the labels come from the data itself
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised clustering

explanation_after: Self-supervised learning generates labels from the data itself (next token to predict). No human labelling is required. This allows training on enormous amounts of unlabelled internet text.

stem: Which learning paradigm is most appropriate for a robotics arm that must learn to grasp objects?

options.text: Supervised learning — just show it thousands of labelled grasps
Unsupervised learning — let it cluster similar objects
Reinforcement learning — reward successful grasps, penalise drops
Transfer learning from a pre-trained image classifier

explanation_after: Robot manipulation involves sequential decisions where feedback (successful grasp or not) is only available after the action. RL's trial-and-error with delayed rewards maps naturally to this problem.

All your data is labelled
You have a small labelled dataset and a large unlabelled dataset
You want to combine two different models

explanation_after: Semi-supervised learning uses a few labelled examples (expensive to obtain) combined with many unlabelled examples (cheap) to train better than supervised learning with labels alone.

stem: Self-supervised learning (like GPT's next-token prediction) is sometimes mistakenly called 'unsupervised learning.' What's the key technical distinction between them?

options.text: There is no real distinction — the two terms describe exactly the same technique
Self-supervised learning still trains with a supervised-style loss against a target derived from the input itself, whereas true unsupervised learning (like clustering) has no target to predict at all
Unsupervised learning always requires more compute than self-supervised learning
Self-supervised learning cannot be implemented with neural networks

explanation_after: Self-supervised learning auto-generates a target from the input (e.g. 'predict the next word') and trains with an ordinary supervised loss comparing the prediction to that target. Unsupervised learning, like k-means clustering, has no target to predict at all — it only uncovers structure. The 'self-supervised' name reflects that labels are auto-generated rather than human-annotated, but mechanically the training is supervised.

stem: A team wants to train a model to predict tomorrow's stock closing price using years of historical data, where the actual price that occurred on every past day is already known. Which learning paradigm fits best, and why not reinforcement learning?

options.text: Reinforcement learning, because the model should be rewarded whenever its prediction is close to correct

Supervised learning — since the correct answer (the actual historical price) already exists for every example, there's no need for the costly trial-and-error exploration reinforcement learning requires
Unsupervised learning, since financial data doesn't really have true labels
Semi-supervised learning, because only some historical prices are considered reliable

explanation_after: When ground-truth outcomes already exist for every input, as with historical prices, supervised learning can use them directly as training targets — far more sample-efficient than reinforcement learning. RL earns its keep when correct answers must be discovered through interaction and delayed reward (like the robot grasping example), not when labelled historical outcomes are already sitting in a dataset.
